doc.title: Helen Oakley Dance interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 12, 1998

title: First hearing jazz as a child in Toronto: Coal Cart Blues
summary: At eight she alone liked the early black blues records the family received; she learned to tell instruments by ear.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Yes. Can you recall when you first heard jazz music and were attracted to it?

Well of course I know Stanley is probably going to wish to argue about this, but I always insist I was in Toronto, which was very corny then, not quite so corny now, but there was jazz, it existed, it wasn’t an elephant, and in those days the family had records in batches once a month, from the big record stores you see, and so about twelve records, which everybody had a chance to approve. And only I would catch on to one, which nobody else liked, and of course it was jazz. And I was eight years old. Stanley wants to argue about that. But to me I was eight years old, I was a child.
Well he wasn’t there, was he?

You know it was my first thing — the first time that I ever said this is who I am. And mother would say, “Well Helen can have her records,” which was always it. And it was Coal Cart Blues by — let’s see my memory fails me all the time — Stanley might be able to mutter things in the background, could he?
Yes. It wasn’t the Original Dixieland Jazz Band was it?
Oh no, no, no. It was black. It was —
It was very, very early. The early, early blues. The first records that I listened to. It was black records. Who was it?
No, it was a band. It wasn’t even Bechet, it was before that.

Yeah, it was back in his days, definitely. And so that was when I was first introduced to jazz. And right away, that was it. And that’s all I wanted to know about, and hear. And I didn’t know what the instruments were or what I was listening to, but I always knew what I was listening to. And years later I said oh that’s Benny Goodman. And then I’d say oh that’s Bunny Berrigan. I knew all those instruments but I didn’t know what they were. I wasn’t a trained musician. But happily I think I might say, like many musicians, I did have ears. And that’s what’s important.
And eventually you were able to tell one player from another.
That’s right. And one instrument from another was very important.
